sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Tislelizumab, an anti–PD-1 monoclonal antibody, is approved for various indications intravenously. Subcutaneous delivery offers potential advantages in convenience and resource utilization. BGB-A317-103 assessed pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of subcutaneous tislelizumab in treatment-naïve patients with advanced or metastatic non–small cell lung cancer.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: BGB-A317-103 is an open-label, multicenter, phase I study. In part 1 (dose/injection site exploration), patients received subcutaneous tislelizumab (abdomen or thigh injections; 300 mg) in two of the first three cycles and intravenous tislelizumab (200 mg) in the remaining cycle, followed by intravenous tislelizumab thereafter. In part 2 (dose expansion), patients received 300 mg of subcutaneous tislelizumab in the thigh in all cycles. Both parts included chemotherapy during the first four to six cycles. Pharmacokinetics, bioavailability, efficacy, immunogenicity, and safety were assessed.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: At data cutoff (December 6, 2024), in part 1 (N = 39), subcutaneous administration yielded higher trough concentrations than intravenous [geometric means: 23.1 μg/mL (thigh), 19.5 μg/mL (abdomen), and 14.8 μg/mL (intravenously)]. Estimated bioavailability was 85.6% for thigh and 72.4% for abdomen. In part 2 (N = 22), subcutaneous tislelizumab in the thigh showed consistent pharmacokinetics with part 1. Preliminary analysis showed an overall response rate of 44.4%; the median duration of response and median progression-free survival were not reached. Tislelizumab’s safety profile was consistent with previous studies, with no new signals or injection-site reactions.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Subcutaneous tislelizumab demonstrated high bioavailability after thigh and abdomen injections. Safety and efficacy were consistent with previous tislelizumab plus chemotherapy studies, warranting further investigation of subcutaneous tislelizumab.

boxed-text.p: The phase I BGB-A317-103 study of subcutaneous tislelizumab in patients with advanced or metastatic non–small cell lung cancer demonstrates the potential for a more convenient administration method, compared with intravenous infusion, of this PD-1 inhibitor. The favorable pharmacokinetic profile, as well as comparable safety and efficacy, suggests that subcutaneous tislelizumab could maintain efficacy while reducing treatment burden for patients. This approach may lead to shorter administration times, improved efficiency at the treatment facility, and the possibility of administration outside of hospital settings. Such advancements could significantly affect patient quality of life and healthcare resource utilization. Moreover, the high bioavailability of subcutaneous tislelizumab, particularly when administered in the thigh, indicates that this route of administration could provide consistent drug exposure between doses. If confirmed in larger studies, subcutaneous tislelizumab could represent a meaningful improvement in immunotherapy delivery, potentially increasing treatment adherence and patient satisfaction while maintaining therapeutic efficacy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitors, including those targeting the PD-1 pathway, have revolutionized cancer treatment across multiple tumor types in recent years. Many patients treated with these agents have experienced improved outcomes, leading to their widespread adoption across multiple oncologic indications (1).

Tislelizumab, a humanized IgG4 monoclonal anti–PD-1 antibody, is in development for the treatment of various solid tumors, both as monotherapy and in combination with other therapies. Patients with various types of solid tumors treated with tislelizumab have experienced improved survival outcomes, leading to its regulatory approval in Europe, the United States, China, and other countries in numerous indications (2–7).

There is growing interest in subcutaneous formulations of immunotherapy agents (8–11). Subcutaneous formulations offer several potential advantages, including simplified drug preparation, shortened administration times, reduced treatment burden for patients, and improved efficiency at treatment facilities, while maintaining efficacy and safety comparable with those of intravenous formulations (12–15). Subcutaneous formulation may allow for safe administration beyond the hospital setting, potentially improving patient quality of life. Moreover, patients have reported a preference for subcutaneous delivery over intravenous infusion (14, 16, 17). Currently, tislelizumab is available only as an intravenous formulation (18, 19); however, a subcutaneous formulation of tislelizumab is in development.

Here, we report the primary results of BGB-A317-103, a phase I, open-label, multicenter clinical trial designed to evaluate the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, efficacy, safety, and tolerability of subcutaneous tislelizumab in the first-line treatment of patients with locally advanced or metastatic non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

sec.title: Study design and treatment
sec.p: BGB-A317-103 was an open-label, multicenter, phase I study conducted in 15 centers across China and Europe. The study comprised two parts: dose/injection-site exploration (part 1) and dose expansion (part 2; Supplementary Fig. S1).

Part 1 evaluated the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, safety, and tolerability of subcutaneous tislelizumab administration. Two subcutaneous injection sites (abdomen and thigh) were evaluated. Patients followed one of six predefined administration sequences in the first three cycles, assigned through an interactive response technology system (Supplementary Table S1). The dose regimen comprised 300 mg of subcutaneous tislelizumab in the thigh or abdomen and 200 mg of intravenous tislelizumab in the first three cycles per the assigned administration sequences. From cycle 4 onward, patients received 200 mg of intravenous tislelizumab once every 3 weeks.
In part 2, patients received the recommended dosage of 300 mg of subcutaneous tislelizumab once every 3 weeks in the thigh, the injection site selected in part 1, for the whole duration of treatment.

In both parts, patients also received histology-based induction chemotherapy during the first four to six cycles. For advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC, induction therapy consisted of cisplatin 75 mg/m2 or carboplatin area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) 5 and pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 i.v. once every 3 weeks on day 1 of the first four to six cycles. This was followed by maintenance therapy with pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 i.v. once every 3 weeks on day 1 of each cycle, starting after the completion of initial combination chemotherapy. Patients with advanced or metastatic squamous NSCLC received induction chemotherapy of carboplatin AUC 5 or 6 (on day 1) plus paclitaxel 175 or 200 mg/m2 (on day 1) or nab-paclitaxel 100 mg/m2 (on days 1, 8, and 15) i.v. every 3 weeks for the first four to six cycles.
Tislelizumab treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, death, or another discontinuation criterion was met, or for a maximum of 24 months, whichever occurred first.

This trial was conducted in accordance with the International Council for Harmonization Good Clinical Practice Guidelines, the Declaration of Helsinki, and all applicable country and local regulations. The protocol was approved by the institutional review board or independent ethics committee at each study site. All patients provided written informed consent prior to being enrolled in this study. The BGB-A317-103 study is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06091943).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: The BGB-A317-103 study enrolled adult patients (≥18 years) with histologically or cytologically confirmed locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC who had not received prior systemic treatment. Key inclusion criteria included at least one measurable lesion as assessed by RECIST v1.1, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of 0 or 1, adequate organ function, and >12 weeks of life expectancy. Key exclusion criteria included NSCLC with actionable mutations (e.g., EGFR-sensitizing mutation, ALK fusion oncogene, BRAFV600E mutation, or ROS1 mutation); active leptomeningeal disease or uncontrolled, untreated brain metastases; active autoimmune diseases or history of autoimmune diseases that may relapse; any malignancy within 5 years before the first dose of study drug (other than NSCLC or any locally recurring cancer that has been treated curatively); and/or a history of interstitial lung disease, noninfectious pneumonitis, or uncontrolled lung diseases.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: In part 1, the primary endpoints were pharmacokinetic characteristics of tislelizumab after subcutaneous administration, including AUC, trough serum concentration (Ctrough), and bioavailability. Secondary endpoints included the maximum serum concentration (Cmax), immunogenicity, safety, and tolerability.

In part 2, the primary endpoints were pharmacokinetic parameters of tislelizumab after subcutaneous administration and safety. Secondary endpoints included immunogenicity, overall response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), and progression-free survival (PFS) as determined from tumor assessments by the investigator per RECIST v1.1.

A noncompartmental analysis was carried out using Phoenix WinNonlin software (Certara, RRID: SCR_003163) to evaluate key pharmacokinetic parameters, AUC, Cmax, Ctrough, and time to Cmax. The pharmacokinetic analyses included only patients with sufficient data to enable the estimation of key pharmacokinetic parameters. In addition, a model-based population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) analysis was conducted on pharmacokinetic data collected in part 1 using a previously developed PopPK model (20) to estimate subcutaneous bioavailability and absorption rate constant.

Safety was assessed through the evaluation of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), serious TEAEs, and laboratory abnormalities reported during the TEAE-reporting period. These were characterized by type, frequency, severity (as graded by NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v5.0), timing, seriousness, and relationship to study therapy.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The sample size for this study was determined based on pharmacologic considerations and was not based on statistical power calculations. Part 1 was designed to enroll approximately 36 patients, with six administration sequences covering all combinations of subcutaneous injection site (abdomen or thigh) and intravenous cycles (cycle 1 to cycle 3). Part 2 was designed to enroll approximately 20 patients.

The pharmacokinetic-evaluable analysis set included all treated patients for whom valid pharmacokinetic parameters were estimated. The efficacy-evaluable analysis set included all dosed patients who had radiologically evaluable disease at baseline and at least one evaluable postbaseline radiologic tumor-response assessment. The immunogenicity-evaluable analysis set included all patients who received at least one dose of tislelizumab and had both baseline and at least one postbaseline antidrug antibody (ADA) results available. The safety-evaluable analysis set included all patients who received at least one dose of tislelizumab.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic, disease characteristics, pharmacokinetic parameters, and safety data. The ORR, disease control rate, and clinical benefit rate were calculated and presented with two-sided exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% confidence intervals (CI). Time-to-event endpoints, PFS and DOR, were analyzed using Kaplan–Meier methodology, with 95% CIs estimated using the Brookmeyer and Crowley method with log–log transformation.

sec.title: Patient demographics and baseline characteristics
sec.p: Between November 2023 and December 2024, 39 patients were enrolled in part 1 of the BGB-A317-103 study. All patients received at least one dose of tislelizumab and were therefore evaluable for the safety assessment. At the data cutoff date (December 6, 2024), the median study follow-up time for part 1 was 8.8 months (range, 1.1–12.3), and 17 of 39 (43.6%) patients remained on treatment (Fig. 1A). The median age was 64 years (range, 47–75 years), 36 of 39 (92.3%) patients were men, 26 of 39 (66.7%) were Asian, and 13 of 39 (33.3%) were White (Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). The median exposure to tislelizumab, regardless of administration route, was 8.1 months (range, 0.7–12.3).

sec.p: Part 2 of the study enrolled 23 patients, and 22 received a minimum of one tislelizumab dose, qualifying them for inclusion in the safety evaluation. At the data cutoff date (December 6, 2024), the median study follow-up time for part 2 was 4.7 months (range, 0.1–6.1), with 16 of 22 patients (72.7%) continuing treatment (Fig. 1B). The median age was 67 years (range, 57–75 years), all patients were men, 13 of 22 (59.1%) were Asian, and nine of 22 (40.9%) were White (Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). The median exposure to subcutaneous tislelizumab was 5.1 months (range, 4.2–6.1).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics and bioavailability
sec.p: For part 1, at the data cutoff date of December 6, 2024, tislelizumab pharmacokinetic data were available for 39 patients (Table 2). Observed Ctrough geometric means for cycle 1 were 23.1 μg/mL for subcutaneous tislelizumab 300 mg in the thigh, 19.5 μg/mL for subcutaneous tislelizumab 300 mg in the abdomen, and 14.8 μg/mL for the 200 mg intravenous infusion reference. Observed cycle 1 Cmax geometric means were 35.6, 28.6, and 73.6 μg/mL for subcutaneous injection in the thigh, subcutaneous injection in the abdomen, and intravenous infusion, respectively (Table 2; Fig. 2). The time to reach maximum concentration (Tmax) was 5.02 days (range, 2.98–13.93 days) for subcutaneous injection in the abdomen and 6.09 days (range, 3–7.05 days) for subcutaneous injection in the thigh. Preliminary PopPK modeling estimated bioavailability of 85.6% (relative standard error 4%) for subcutaneous injection in the thigh and 72.4% (relative standard error 6.2%) for subcutaneous injection in the abdomen. Based on these findings, the 300 mg subcutaneous injection of tislelizumab in the thigh was chosen as the recommended dosage for part 2 of the study.

sec.p: For part 2, at the data cutoff date of December 6, 2024, tislelizumab pharmacokinetic data were available for 21 patients who received 300 mg tislelizumab via subcutaneous injection in the thigh once every 3 weeks (Table 2). Tislelizumab exhibited approximately threefold accumulation with repeated subcutaneous dosing in the thigh. The observed geometric mean Ctrough was 23.5 μg/mL and 64.9 μg/mL, Cmax was 38.3 μg/mL and 102.1 μg/mL, and AUC0–21d was 649 day·μg/mL and 1,776 day·μg/mL at cycles 1 and 5, respectively. The Tmax was 5.04 days (range, 2.91–14 days) in cycle 1 and 5 days (range, 2.95–7.04 days) in cycle 5. In general, observed tislelizumab cycle 1 exposures were comparable between parts 1 and 2 of the study and similar or higher than those observed at the 200 mg intravenous dose.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Efficacy assessments were conducted according to the protocol-specified endpoints in part 2 of the study for patients receiving subcutaneous tislelizumab in the thigh. With only one PFS event observed among 18 evaluable patients, the median PFS was not reached [95% CI, not estimable (NE)–NE]. The ORR was 44.4% (95% CI, 21.5%–69.2%). Among patients who achieved a confirmed objective response, the median DOR was not reached (95% CI, NE–NE).

sec.title: Immunogenicity
sec.p: Immunogenicity was assessed by measuring the incidence and titers of anti-tislelizumab antibodies. At baseline, 2.7% (one of 37) of patients in part 1 and none in part 2 receiving subcutaneous tislelizumab had a positive anti-tislelizumab sample. A total of 15 of 37 patients (40.5%) in part 1 and 11 of 20 patients (55%) in part 2 tested positive for treatment-emergent ADAs. None of the patients tested positive for neutralizing antibodies. To evaluate the potential impact of ADAs on tislelizumab exposure, pharmacokinetic profiles between ADA-positive and ADA-negative groups were compared. The comparison showed that the pharmacokinetic profiles were comparable between the two groups.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: In the safety-evaluable analysis set of 39 patients in part 1, 66.7% (26 of 39) experienced grade ≥3 TEAEs. The investigators assessed that 25.6% (10 of 39) of patients had grade ≥3 TEAEs related to tislelizumab. One fatal TEAE was reported and deemed unrelated to treatment. Serious TEAEs were experienced by 38.5% (15 of 39) of patients, with 20.5% (eight of 39) of patients experiencing serious TEAEs assessed by the investigator to be related to tislelizumab. TEAEs leading to discontinuation of tislelizumab occurred in 15.4% (six of 39) of patients, with 12.8% (five of 39) of patients experiencing tislelizumab-related TEAEs leading to discontinuation. Treatment modifications due to TEAEs were observed in 61.5% (24 of 39) of patients, with 51.3% (20 of 39) of patients experiencing TEAEs that led to tislelizumab treatment modification (Table 3).

sec.p: In part 1, the most common adverse events were anemia and decreased neutrophil count, occurring in 66.7% (26 of 39) and 56.4% (22 of 39) of patients, respectively. Grade ≥3 events of anemia and decreased neutrophil count were observed in 23.1% (nine of 39) and 43.6% (17 of 39) of patients, respectively. These were followed by decreased white blood cell count in 53.8% (21 of 39) of patients, with grade ≥3 events in 17.9% (seven of 39) of patients (Supplementary Table S3). Immune-mediated adverse events (imAEs) were experienced by 41% (16 of 39) of patients; three (7.7%) patients experienced a grade ≥3 imAE, specifically Stevens–Johnson syndrome, immune-mediated lung disease, and drug-induced liver injury (Table 4). No subcutaneous injection-site reactions were reported.

sec.p: In the safety-evaluable analysis set of 22 patients in part 2, 59.1% (13 of 22) experienced grade ≥3 TEAEs. The investigators assessed that 27.3% (six of 22) of patients had grade ≥3 TEAEs related to tislelizumab. Two fatal TEAEs were reported and deemed unrelated to treatment. Serious TEAEs were experienced by 27.3% (six of 22) of patients, with 13.6% (three of 22) of patients experiencing serious TEAEs assessed by the investigator to be related to tislelizumab. TEAEs leading to discontinuation of tislelizumab occurred in 4.5% (one of 22) of patients and were not related to tislelizumab. Treatment modifications due to TEAEs were observed in 54.5% (12 of 22) of patients, with 36.4% (eight of 22) of patients experiencing TEAEs that led to tislelizumab treatment modification (Table 3).

Similar to part 1, in part 2, the most common TEAEs were anemia and decreased neutrophil count, both occurring in 68.2% (15 of 22) of patients, and decreased white blood cell count, occurring in 45.5% (10 of 22) of patients. Grade ≥3 TEAEs for these were observed in 9.1% (two of 22), 36.4% (eight of 22), and 13.6% (three of 22) of patients, respectively (Supplementary Table S3). imAEs were experienced by 22.7% (five of 22) of patients; two (9.1%) experienced a grade ≥3 imAE, namely colitis and diabetes mellitus (Table 4). No subcutaneous injection-site reaction occurred in part 2 of the study.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This phase I study evaluated the pharmacokinetic profile, bioavailability, efficacy, safety, and tolerability of subcutaneous tislelizumab in previously untreated patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC. The results demonstrate that the subcutaneous administration of tislelizumab at a 300-mg dose provides comparable exposure compared with intravenous administration of tislelizumab at a 200-mg dose, with a safety profile consistent with previous studies of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy (21, 22).

The pharmacokinetic analysis showed that subcutaneous administration in both the thigh and abdomen resulted in higher Ctrough values compared with intravenous administration, with geometric means of 23.1 and 19.5 μg/mL for thigh and abdomen subcutaneous injections, respectively, versus 14.8 μg/mL after intravenous dose. This suggests that subcutaneous administration may provide more consistent drug exposure between doses compared with intravenous administration. The subcutaneous thigh injection site demonstrated slightly higher exposure compared with the abdominal site, with estimated bioavailability of 85.6% for the subcutaneous thigh injection versus 72.4% for the subcutaneous abdomen injection. Consequently, the subcutaneous thigh injection of 300 mg tislelizumab was selected as the recommended dose for part 2 of the study. In part 2, the preliminary efficacy of subcutaneous tislelizumab was evaluated. The median PFS was not reached, and the ORR was 44.4% for subcutaneous thigh administration, with the median DOR not reached at data cutoff. Immunogenicity assessments revealed treatment-emergent ADAs in 55% of patients receiving subcutaneous tislelizumab, but none of the patients tested positive for neutralizing antibodies. Notably, the incidence of ADAs does not seem to affect the pharmacokinetic exposure of tislelizumab as evidenced by the comparable pharmacokinetic profiles between patients who tested positive for ADAs and patients who tested negative for ADAs. Overall, these results suggest that subcutaneous tislelizumab demonstrates clinical activity in this patient population while potentially providing greater convenience for patients and healthcare providers.

These findings are similar to those observed with other subcutaneous formulations of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (10, 23, 24). Patient exposure to atezolizumab via subcutaneous injection was comparable with intravenous administration, with estimated bioavailability of 82.9% in the thigh and 71.1% in the abdomen (23). Subcutaneous atezolizumab, compared with intravenous, demonstrated similar efficacy (PFS: HR, 1.08; ORR: subcutaneous 12% vs. intravenous 10%) and immunogenicity (incidence of ADAs: subcutaneous 19.5% vs. intravenous 13.9%; ref. 10). Bioavailability for subcutaneous nivolumab was estimated at 76.7% (24). The CheckMate 67T study and IMscin001 study reported an injection-site reaction rate of 7.3% among patients receiving subcutaneous nivolumab (9) and 4.5% for patients receiving subcutaneous atezolizumab, respectively (10).

The safety profile of subcutaneous tislelizumab was consistent with the known safety profile of intravenous tislelizumab, with no new safety signals identified. No injection-site reactions were reported in this study, which represents a potentially favorable characteristic of subcutaneous tislelizumab administration. The incidence and types of imAEs were also consistent with previous tislelizumab studies, with no new safety signals emerging with subcutaneous administration. We observed a higher incidence of grade ≥3 TEAEs and imAEs in part 1 compared with that in part 2. This difference is likely attributable to the longer median exposure to tislelizumab in part 1 versus part 2, the longer overall follow-up period in part 1, and differences in baseline characteristics between cohorts, particularly the higher proportion of squamous histology in part 2 and associated differences in chemotherapy regimens. The mixed administration regimen in part 1 also complicates attribution of events to specific routes of administration. These results support further investigation of subcutaneous tislelizumab in a larger study.

Limitations of this study should be noted. The sample size was relatively small as is typical for early-phase trials. Additionally, the follow-up time was limited; therefore, long-term safety and efficacy data are not yet available. We acknowledge that the significant sex imbalance in our study population (95.1% male) may limit the generalizability of our findings. The predominance of male participants might have contributed to the higher proportion of squamous histology observed, although based on the broader tislelizumab clinical program in NSCLC, treatment efficacy seems consistent across sexes despite histologic differences. We acknowledge that PD-L1 expression data were not collected in this phase I study, which limits our ability to evaluate the relationship between PD-L1 status and treatment outcomes with subcutaneous tislelizumab. In the ongoing phase III trial of subcutaneous tislelizumab, PD-L1 expression data are being prospectively collected, and their correlation with clinical outcomes will be comprehensively evaluated. Larger studies with longer follow-ups will be needed to fully characterize the clinical profile of subcutaneous tislelizumab.

This phase I study demonstrates that subcutaneous tislelizumab has favorable pharmacokinetic characteristics and a safety profile consistent with previous studies of tislelizumab plus chemotherapy. The observed Ctrough levels support the potential for effective dosing with a subcutaneous formulation. Although the preliminary efficacy findings are encouraging, these results warrant further investigation of subcutaneous tislelizumab in a phase III trial. If confirmed in larger studies, subcutaneous tislelizumab could offer a more convenient treatment option for patients while maintaining the efficacy and safety of intravenous administration.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: On request and subject to certain criteria, conditions, and exceptions, BeOne Medicines, Ltd. will provide access to individual deidentified participant data from applicable BeOne Medicines–sponsored studies. BeOne Medicines shares data only when permitted by applicable data privacy and security laws and regulations, shares when it is feasible to do so without compromising the privacy of the study participants, and other considerations. Data requests may be submitted to ClinicalTrials@beonemed.com. The study presented in this article meets the criteria for an applicable BeOne Medicines–sponsored study.
